Usury is the practice of lending money and charging the borrower an unreasonably high rate of interest — interest so excessive that it is exploitative, meaning it unfairly takes advantage of the person who borrowed the money.

To understand usury properly, you first need to be clear on what interest is. When someone lends you money, they often charge you a fee for the privilege of using their money. That fee, expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed, is called interest. For example, if you borrow $100 and pay back $110, the extra $10 is interest. This is a normal, accepted part of how finance works. Usury is not just interest — it is interest taken too far, beyond what is fair or legal.
What Makes Interest Cross the Line Into Usury?

This is the most important distinction to understand. Not all interest is usury. The line is crossed when the interest rate is:

  • Excessively high — far beyond what other lenders charge or what the market considers reasonable.
  • Exploitative — deliberately targeting people who are desperate, vulnerable, or have no other options, knowing they will accept almost any terms just to get the money.
  • Illegal — in many countries and states, the law sets a maximum interest rate that lenders are allowed to charge. Charging above that cap is usury by legal definition, regardless of whether both parties agreed to it.

A simple way to think about it: if a bank charges you 8% interest on a loan, that is normal lending. If a street-level moneylender charges you 200% interest on the same loan, knowing you are desperate and have nowhere else to turn, that is usury.

Imagine you urgently need $500 to pay a medical bill. You have bad credit, so no bank will lend to you. A lender approaches you and says, "I'll give you $500 today, but in one month you must pay me back $700." That's $200 in interest on a $500 loan in just 30 days — an annualized interest rate of nearly 500%. You agree because you have no choice. This is the essence of usury: an obscene rate of interest charged to someone in a vulnerable position who has little power to negotiate otherwise.
The Two Lives of This Word: Historical and Modern

The word usury has meant slightly different things across history, and understanding both meanings gives you the full picture.

Historically, usury meant any charging of interest at all — zero exceptions. For a long period in Western and Middle Eastern history, the major religions (Christianity, Islam, and Judaism all, at various points in time) considered it morally wrong to profit from lending money. The thinking was: if someone is in need and you help them, you should not profit from their hardship. Under this view, even a 1% interest rate was considered usury.

In the modern world, this strict religious view has largely been set aside in legal and commercial life. Society now accepts that charging interest is a legitimate part of banking and lending. So today, usury specifically refers to interest that is excessive and/or above the legal maximum — not just any interest. This is the meaning you'll encounter in newspapers, law, and everyday conversation today.

So in summary: the meaning has narrowed over time — from "any interest" to "unfair or illegal interest."

Because usury is harmful, most legal systems have created usury laws — rules that cap the maximum interest rate a lender can legally charge. These laws exist to protect borrowers, especially the most financially vulnerable ones, from being crushed by unpayable debt. If a lender violates these caps, the consequences can include the loan being declared void, the lender being forced to refund the excess interest collected, and criminal or civil penalties.

It helps to understand why societies treat usury as a serious wrong, not just a minor overstep:

  • It traps people in debt. When interest rates are extreme, borrowers often cannot pay off the principal (the original amount borrowed) because all their payments are consumed by interest. The debt never shrinks — it grows.
  • It targets the vulnerable. Usurers typically do not target wealthy people who have options. They target people who are desperate — those facing job loss, illness, or poverty — who will accept any terms.
  • It transfers wealth upward. Money flows from the poorest borrowers to wealthy lenders at an accelerating rate, deepening inequality.
  • It is coercive in spirit, even if technically consensual. A person who "agrees" to a 400% interest rate because they have no alternative has not really made a free choice. Usury exploits the absence of choice.
Usury in the Modern World: Where You'll See It

Even with usury laws in place, usury-like practices exist under different names:

  • Payday loans — short-term loans, often at annualized rates of 300–600%, marketed to low-income people who need cash before their next paycheck.
  • Loan sharks — illegal, unlicensed lenders who charge enormous rates and sometimes use threats or violence to collect repayment.
  • Predatory lending — a broader term for any lending practice that imposes unfair or abusive terms on borrowers, which may or may not technically exceed the legal usury cap.

These are all modern descendants of what has historically been called usury.

If you ever need to summarize it: Usury is the practice of lending money at an interest rate so high that it is exploitative — and in legal terms, it means charging interest above the maximum rate permitted by law.
